title: Melt-and-pour bar soap
subtitle: The lye-free route for beginners
excerpt: A melt-and-pour bar soap using a ready-made glycerin base, scented and coloured to taste. No lye handling required, the base is already fully saponified, leaving only the creative work of adding fragrance, colour, and botanicals. Makes four bars in about 40 minutes; ready to use the same day.
sourceNotes: Melt-and-pour soap base: glycerin-dominant premade base; fully saponified at manufacture. Common base types include clear glycerin, opaque shea, and olive oil variants, choose based on the finished bar transparency required. Fragrance oil usage rate: 2-3% of base weight is standard for M&P; higher percentages can cause sweating on the surface. Mica/soap-safe dyes: use cosmetic-grade only; craft shop dyes may bleed or discolour.

recipe.batchNotes: Scale directly, ratios hold. Double the base for 8 bars. The only limit is the size of your moulds and your microwave-safe pouring jug.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: M&P soap bars are ready to use the same day once fully set. They can be wrapped individually in cling film to prevent surface sweating and stored for up to 6 months.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: 6 months unwrapped; up to a year if individually wrapped in cling film to prevent surface sweating. Discard if the bar develops mould (unlikely but possible if heavily botanically decorated and stored damp) or smells off.

glossaryTerms.definition: A soap-making method using a pre-saponified glycerin base that is melted, customised, and poured into moulds. No lye handling is involved because the saponification was done at manufacture.

The chemical reaction between lye (sodium or potassium hydroxide) and fat or oil that produces soap and glycerin. In melt-and-pour bases, this process is done at the factory, so no lye handling is needed at home.

content.text: Melt-and-pour soap uses a ready-made glycerin base that has already been through the lye-and-fat

process at the factory. You melt it, stir in fragrance oil and colour, and pour it into moulds. No lye handling, no cure time, no safety equipment beyond oven gloves for the hot jug. Four bars; ready to use in about an hour.

This is the route for someone new to soap-making who wants to practise scent and colour combinations before committing to the full cold-process method. The finished bar is a genuine soap, not a detergent cake, it lathers well and rinses clean.

items.prepNote: clear glycerin base; fully saponified at manufacture; no lye handling needed
your choice of soap-safe fragrance oil at 2.5% of base weight; add below 70°C
soap-safe mica powder or liquid soap dye; adjust to desired colour intensity

content.text: Cut the soap base into rough 2 cm cubes and place in a microwave-safe jug. Microwave in 30-second bursts on medium power, stirring between each burst, until fully melted. The base is ready when it is clear and liquid with no solid lumps.
Let the melted base cool to about 60°C before adding the fragrance oil, above 70°C some fragrance compounds start to evaporate. Stir the fragrance in gently; avoid whipping in air bubbles.

Add the colour a little at a time, stirring until evenly distributed. For a clear bar, a small pinch of mica gives a translucent tinted effect; for an opaque bar, switch to a shea or milk base rather than the clear glycerin.
Pour into the moulds slowly to minimise surface bubbles. If any bubbles form on top, spritz briefly with rubbing alcohol from a small spray bottle, the bubbles collapse immediately.
If using dried botanicals, press them gently onto the top surface of the bar once a thin skin has formed, about 5 minutes after pouring.
Leave the moulds undisturbed at room temperature for at least 1 hour before unmoulding. The bars are ready to use as soon as they are fully set.

Clear glycerin gives a translucent, jewel-like bar. Opaque shea or goat milk bases give a white or cream bar more similar in appearance to cold-process soap. Olive oil bases are softer and take longer to set. All are interchangeable in this recipe, adjust the mould type to suit the base hardness (firm silicone moulds work for all; softer craft moulds suit harder bases).

Wrap finished bars individually in cling film to prevent the glycerin surface from sweating in humid air. Stored this way, they keep up to a year. Unwrapped, they're fine for 6 months in a cool, dry place.
bars don't go rancid the way cold-process bars can, but botanical decorations on the surface can grow mould if stored damp. Keep them dry.
